title: Signed or Plain char?
prompt:
Plain `char` signedness is implementation-defined. On a typical x86-64 Linux box plain char is signed; on this machine it is not — implementation-defined means the platform decides and your code must adapt. Implement `void program(void)` that prints two lines:
 
```
plain char: <signed|unsigned — derived>
min value: <CHAR_MIN>
```
 
Derive BOTH facts at runtime: assign `(char)-1` and compare with -1 (signed) or 255 (unsigned), then print `CHAR_MIN` from `<limits.h>`. Your output here may differ from x86-64 — that difference is the lesson.

tests.name: derived signedness
tests.code:
const char* out = cj_capture(program);
char probe = (char)-1; CHECK_CONTAINS(out, probe == -1 ? "signed" : "unsigned");
tests.hint: The test derives the platform truth the same way your code must: probe == -1 means signed, probe == 255 means unsigned.

tests.name: exact two-line output
tests.hint: sprintf builds the platform-truth expectation from probe and CHAR_MIN, then the program must match it exactly — hard-coding either line fails somewhere.
